questions.q: Which statement best explains why the first ionisation energy decreases from magnesium to barium?

options.A: The nuclear charge decreases down the group, so the outer electrons are held less strongly.
options.B: Each atom has more electrons in its outer shell, and they repel each other more.
options.C: The shielding stays the same down the group, but the outer electrons are in a higher-energy d sub-shell.
options.D: The outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.

questions.solution: Down the group each atom has an extra shell, so the outer s electrons are further from the nucleus and better shielded by inner electrons. These effects outweigh the rise in nuclear charge, so less energy is needed to remove an outer electron. (The nuclear charge increases, it does not decrease; every Group 2 atom has two outer electrons.)

questions.q: Why does the reactivity of the Group 2 metals with water increase down the group?

options.A: Less energy is needed to remove the two outer electrons to form the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion.
options.B: The atoms gain electrons more easily to form negative ions.
options.C: The metallic bonding becomes stronger down the group.
options.D: The hydroxides formed become less soluble down the group.

questions.solution: Group 2 metals react by losing their two outer electrons. Down the group the first and second ionisation energies fall, so the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion forms more easily and the metal reacts faster. (Metals lose electrons; they do not gain them. The hydroxides actually become more soluble down the group.)

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon is heated in steam. Which are the products?

options.A: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\)
options.B: \(\mathrm{MgO(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\)
options.C: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\)
options.D: \(\mathrm{MgO(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\)

questions.solution: With steam, magnesium burns with a bright white flame: \(\mathrm{Mg(s) + H_{2}O(g) \rightarrow MgO(s) + H_{2}(g)}\). The products are magnesium oxide and hydrogen. (The hydroxide forms with cold water, very slowly; the gas is always hydrogen, never oxygen.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the melting point of the Group 2 metals generally decreases from calcium to barium?

options.A: The metal ions get larger, so the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons gets weaker.
options.B: Each atom releases fewer delocalised electrons down the group.
options.C: The London forces between the atoms get weaker down the group.
options.D: The ionic bonds between the atoms get weaker as the ions get larger.

questions.solution: Group 2 metals have metallic bonding: a lattice of \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Every atom gives two electrons, but the ions get larger down the group, so the electrons are further from the ion centres and the attraction is weaker. (The metals do not have London forces or ionic bonds between their atoms.)

questions.q: Which pair shows the most soluble hydroxide and the least soluble sulfate of the elements magnesium to barium?

options.A: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\)
options.B: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\)
options.C: \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\)
options.D: \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\)

questions.solution: The two trends go in opposite directions. Hydroxides become more soluble down the group, so \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) is the most soluble. Sulfates become less soluble down the group, so \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\) is the least soluble (it is insoluble). (\(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) is only sparingly soluble.)

questions.q: Dilute sodium hydroxide solution is added to separate solutions containing \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ions and \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) ions. What is seen?

options.A: A white precipitate with both solutions.
options.B: No visible change with \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\); a white precipitate with \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\).
options.C: A white precipitate with \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\); no visible change with \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\).
options.D: No visible change with either solution.

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) is sparingly soluble, so it precipitates as a white solid. \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\) is the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide, so it stays in solution. (The pattern is reversed for the sulfates, where barium gives the precipitate.)

questions.q: The same amounts of magnesium oxide and barium oxide are added to separate beakers of water. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The magnesium oxide gives the solution with the higher pH, because magnesium hydroxide is more soluble.
options.B: Both solutions have pH 7, because Group 2 oxides do not react with water.
options.C: The barium oxide gives the solution with the lower pH, because barium is the more reactive metal.
options.D: The barium oxide gives the solution with the higher pH, because barium hydroxide is more soluble.

questions.solution: Both oxides react with water to form hydroxides, for example \(\mathrm{BaO + H_{2}O \rightarrow Ba(OH)_{2}}\). Hydroxide solubility increases down the group, so the barium solution has the higher concentration of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions and the higher pH. (Magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble, giving a pH of only about 9 to 10.)

questions.q: In the test for sulfate ions, why is the barium chloride solution acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.A: To dissolve the barium sulfate precipitate so that it can be seen more clearly.
options.B: To remove carbonate ions, which would also give a white precipitate with barium ions.
options.C: To provide chloride ions, which react with the sulfate ions.
options.D: To stop the barium chloride decomposing in solution.

questions.solution: Carbonate ions would form white barium carbonate, a false positive. The acid removes them as carbon dioxide: \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-} + 2H^{+} \rightarrow CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\). Barium sulfate is insoluble in acid, so it still precipitates. (Sulfuric acid must never be used, because it adds sulfate ions.)

questions.q: Barium ions are toxic, yet patients swallow a suspension of barium sulfate before an X-ray of the gut. Why is this safe?

options.A: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so very few \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) ions are absorbed into the blood.
options.B: Stomach acid converts barium sulfate into barium chloride, which is harmless.
options.C: Barium ions are only toxic when they are combined with chloride ions.
options.D: Barium sulfate is absorbed quickly and leaves the body before it can do harm.

questions.solution: Because \(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}\) is insoluble, almost no \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) ions dissolve to be absorbed. It stays in the gut, where it absorbs X-rays and shows the gut's outline. (Barium chloride is soluble and toxic, so conversion to it would be dangerous.)

questions.q: An indigestion tablet contains 0.350 g of magnesium hydroxide (\(M_{\text{r}} = 58.3\)). What volume of \(0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid can it neutralise?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2} + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_{2} + 2H_{2}O}\). Amount of \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}\) = 0.350 ÷ 58.3 = 0.00600 mol, so HCl = 2 × 0.00600 = 0.0120 mol. Volume = 0.0120 ÷ 0.100 = \(0.120\ \text{dm}^{3}\) = \(120\ \text{cm}^{3}\). (Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio leads to 60.0.)

questions.q: Power stations remove sulfur dioxide from their flue gases by passing them through calcium oxide. Why does calcium oxide remove sulfur dioxide?

options.A: Calcium oxide reduces sulfur dioxide to solid sulfur, which is collected.
options.B: Calcium oxide catalyses the decomposition of sulfur dioxide into sulfur and oxygen.
options.C: Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and sulfur dioxide is an acidic oxide, so they react to form a salt, \(\mathrm{CaSO_{3}}\).
options.D: Calcium oxide dissolves the sulfur dioxide without reacting with it.

questions.solution: It is an acid–base reaction: \(\mathrm{CaO(s) + SO_{2}(g) \rightarrow CaSO_{3}(s)}\). The solid calcium sulfite is removed. Sulfur keeps the oxidation number +4, so no reduction takes place. (Calcium carbonate is used in the same way, also giving \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).)

questions.q: What is the minimum mass of calcium oxide (\(M_{\text{r}} = 56.1\)) needed to remove 3.20 tonnes of sulfur dioxide (\(M_{\text{r}} = 64.1\))?

options.A: 1.40 tonnes
options.B: 2.80 tonnes
options.C: 3.66 tonnes
options.D: 5.00 tonnes

questions.solution: \(\mathrm{CaO + SO_{2} \rightarrow CaSO_{3}}\): a 1 : 1 ratio. The mass of CaO is 3.20 × \(\frac{56.1}{64.1}\) = 2.80 tonnes. (Inverting the ratio leads to 3.66 tonnes; using calcium carbonate's \(M_{\text{r}}\) of 100.1 leads to 5.00 tonnes.)

questions.q: Titanium is extracted from titanium(IV) chloride using magnesium. Which shows the equation and the role of the magnesium?

options.A: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\); magnesium is the oxidising agent.
options.B: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + Mg \rightarrow Ti + MgCl_{4}}\); magnesium is the reducing agent.
options.C: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\); magnesium is a catalyst.
options.D: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\); magnesium is the reducing agent.

questions.solution: Magnesium forms \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), so two Mg are needed for the four chloride ions: \(\mathrm{TiCl_{4} + 2Mg \rightarrow Ti + 2MgCl_{2}}\). Mg goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised), and Ti from +4 to 0 (reduced), so magnesium is the reducing agent. (It is used up, so it is not a catalyst.)

questions.q: Which carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature?

options.A: \(\mathrm{MgCO_{3}}\)
options.B: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\)
options.C: \(\mathrm{BaCO_{3}}\)

questions.solution: Thermal stability increases down Group 2, and Group 1 carbonates (except lithium's) do not decompose at Bunsen temperatures. The \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion is the smallest 2+ ion, so it polarises the carbonate ion most, and \(\mathrm{MgCO_{3}}\) decomposes most easily. (Barium carbonate is the most stable Group 2 carbonate.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates increases down the group?

options.A: The metal gets more reactive, so it holds the carbonate ion more strongly.
options.B: The cation gets larger, so its charge density falls and it polarises the carbonate ion less.
options.C: The carbonate ion gets larger down the group, so it is harder to distort.
options.D: The charge on the cation increases down the group, so the lattice is stronger.

questions.solution: All the cations are 2+, but they get larger down the group, so their charge density falls. A less polarising cation distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less, so its C–O bonds are weakened less and more heat is needed to release \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\). (The carbonate ion is the same in every compound.)

questions.q: Which equation shows the thermal decomposition of potassium nitrate?

options.A: \(\mathrm{2KNO_{3} \rightarrow 2KNO_{2} + O_{2}}\)
options.B: \(\mathrm{4KNO_{3} \rightarrow 2K_{2}O + 4NO_{2} + O_{2}}\)
options.C: \(\mathrm{2KNO_{3} \rightarrow 2K + 2NO_{2} + O_{2}}\)
options.D: \(\mathrm{2KNO_{3} \rightarrow K_{2}CO_{3} + 2NO_{2}}\)

questions.solution: Group 1 nitrates (except lithium nitrate) decompose only to the nitrite and oxygen: \(\mathrm{2KNO_{3} \rightarrow 2KNO_{2} + O_{2}}\). (Forming the oxide, \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) is the pattern for Group 2 nitrates and lithium nitrate.)

questions.q: A white solid is either sodium nitrate or magnesium nitrate. Which observation on heating shows that it is magnesium nitrate?

options.A: A gas that relights a glowing splint is given off.
options.B: A gas that turns limewater milky is given off.
options.C: The solid melts before it decomposes.
options.D: A brown gas is given off.

questions.solution: Magnesium nitrate gives brown nitrogen dioxide: \(\mathrm{2Mg(NO_{3})_{2} \rightarrow 2MgO + 4NO_{2} + O_{2}}\). Sodium nitrate gives only oxygen, so both relight a glowing splint and that does not tell them apart. (Neither gives carbon dioxide.)

questions.q: 3.71 g of magnesium nitrate (\(M_{\text{r}} = 148.3\)) is heated until it has fully decomposed. What mass of solid remains? (\(M_{\text{r}}\) of MgO = 40.3)
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{2Mg(NO_{3})_{2} \rightarrow 2MgO + 4NO_{2} + O_{2}}\): one MgO for each \(\mathrm{Mg(NO_{3})_{2}}\). Amount = 3.71 ÷ 148.3 = 0.0250 mol, so the mass of MgO = 0.0250 × 40.3 = 1.01 g. (2.70 g is the mass lost as gases, not the solid left.)

questions.q: A compound gives a pale green flame in a flame test. Which ion does it contain?

options.A: \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\)
options.B: \(\mathrm{Sr^{2+}}\)
options.C: \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\)

questions.solution: Barium compounds give a pale (apple) green flame. Calcium gives orange-red (brick red), strontium crimson and potassium lilac. (Do not confuse barium with strontium: both are low in Group 2, but only barium is green.)

questions.q: Which statement explains how a metal compound produces a characteristic flame colour?

options.A: Electrons are removed completely from the atoms, and the ions formed glow with a particular colour.
options.B: Electrons are excited to higher energy levels by the heat, then fall back, emitting light of particular frequencies.
options.C: The metal reacts with oxygen in the flame, and the energy released is given out as visible light.
options.D: Electrons absorb some frequencies of visible light, and the light that is not absorbed is seen.

questions.solution: Heat promotes electrons to higher energy levels. When they drop back, they emit energy as light; each energy gap fixes a frequency, so the emitted colours are characteristic of the metal. (Absorbing light and seeing what is left is how transition metal complexes are coloured, not flame colours.)
